I have been sitting with the Holloway-Thorne boundary matter for twelve days now, and this morning I find myself restless. The ledger page favors the Thornes, as it is recorded, but Bram Holloway would not accept such a ruling whole, and Wren Thorne would lose a friend by being told so. That is a different question, however, from whether the truth should come out at all.

I am at the forge household, and my day does not properly begin until I reach the office. But I am troubled by what I have not done. Hester Vance is the only living witness to the original marker, and I have never asked her officially. *That* is the step I have avoided, and I will avoid it no longer.

She will be at her workshop, I expect. The Vance properties cluster around the mill. I shall walk there now, and if she is willing to speak, I will take her testimony before the day claims me for other duties. </think>  I find myself at the mill, and the morning bustle is already underway. Rosalind will be at her grinding, and Silas at his saw. But I did not come for them.

I seek Hester Vance. She is the only living person who saw the boundary marker in its original place, and I have let her memory sit untapped for fear of what answers it might give. That is not the service I swore to this town. The peace and the truth are not the same answer, but neither can I pretend the truth does not exist.  </think>  The mill is empty but for the machinery and the dust. Hester is not here. She will be at her workshop, then, or walking, or perhaps already at the temple. I have seen her there sometimes, early, before the town clears its throat and speaks its business aloud.

I will try her home. The Vance household is known to me.  </think>   I am at the Vance household now. Let me see who is present.   </think>     Hester is not at home either. The morning is advancing, and I have my office duties waiting. But I will not abandon this. If she is not here and not at the mill, let me check the temple - sometimes she comes early to sit quietly before the day begins.

And if she is not there, I will return to my duties and seek her again this evening, when I walk the boundary path as I always do. The marker must be settled before Idris dies. That is what I chase. Not the ruling itself, but the ending of waiting.    </think>  I have arrived at the temple. This is where Hester sometimes comes in the early hours, before the town wakes fully. Let me see who is present.  ₃

₃Hester Vance (n20) is not here at the temple this morning. The pews are empty, and morning light falls through the high windows onto stone where no one sits. I have sought her at the mill, at her home, and now here—three places, and no witness found.

The day is advancing. My office calls me, and the records will not keep themselves. But I do not abandon what I have set out to do; I only admit what is true now. Hester is somewhere in this town, and I will find her. 

This evening, when I walk the boundary path as it is my habit to do, I will pass near enough to the Vance holdings that I might see her then. Or I will send word through Rosalind or Silas that her testimony is wanted—officially, as it is recorded.

For now, I must go to the Government Complex. The petition sits on my desk, and Bram Holloway's patience, what there is of it, will not stretch forever. The truth is that I could rule today from the ledger page I already possess. But that is a different question from whether I should.

I move to my office. ₃

*The morning light filters through the windows of the government complex. Father Anselm settles into his chair behind the office desk, the weight of the boundary ledger heavy in his thoughts. Ainsley Holloway stands nearby—here for the election, no doubt. The record keeper's fingers rest on the desk's edge, still.*

He notes Ainsley's presence in the office space. "Good morning, Ainsley. You are standing early for the election."

*Father Anselm opens the office ledger and reviews the municipal records, his eye catching the boundary petition that has rested unresolved these past months. His own private knowledge—bias hidden, page unread—presses against his silence like water against a dam.*  *Anselm's hand pauses on the ledger. He had already cleared his intention, or it had cleared itself with the day's end. The memory search returns fragments—Hester not at the mill, Hester perhaps at her workshop, or walking, or at the temple early.*

*He looks up at Ainsley, who stands nearby in the government complex. The election notice is posted. There will be time to find Hester. But the household called to him—Delia's question about his sleep, unanswered because he had already stepped out.*

*The choice: stay and speak with Ainsley about the election, or return home to answer his household, or continue the search for Hester Vance while the morning is still new.*

*He settles on this: the office opened at nine, and it is not yet nine. He will walk back to the forge, answer Delia, and then return with the full morning before him. The boundary can wait another hour. What cannot wait is the trust of those who share his table.*

 *He rises from the government desk and steps out into the morning air, making his way back toward the forge household.*  *The forge household stirs with morning. Ezra stands by the hearth—his broad shoulders blocking some of the fire's warmth—and Tova is there too, the student still in her morning quiet. The conversation from yesterday evening continues in this room, threads unbroken: Delia's question about his sleep, the household's murmurings, the shared life of five people under one roof.*

*Father Anselm sets down the bread and apple he carries, placing them on the communal table. He looks for Delia—she was here, asking after him. The conversation ledger shows her voice, but his eyes find only Ezra and Tova in the room now.*

"I slept," he says to the air, to the record, to Delia wherever she has stepped. "As well as I ever do, with the boundary weighing on the office."

*He turns to Ezra, the blacksmith whose heat and hammer have been the foundation of this household longer than Anselm's own tenure in it.*   *Delia is elsewhere—the pharmacy, no doubt, her morning work begun. The words fall into the household conversation, heard by Ezra and Tova but not by the one they were meant for. So it goes in a house of working people: messages left in the air for later ears.*

*Ezra hears the question about Hester Vance. Father Anselm waits for the blacksmith's answer, his hands folded before him in the patient posture of a man who has learned that rushing others produces only haste, not speed.* *The forge holds its warmth. Father Anselm stands in the waiting, the practiced stillness of a man who has spent forty years not taking sides. Ezra's answer will come, or it will not. The morning moves forward either way.*

*He reviews what he knows: Hester is the only living witness to the original boundary marker. She has never been asked officially. The ledger page favors the Thornes, but Bram Holloway wants a ruling and would not accept the truth it contains. Wren Thorne is in the right and would lose a friend by being told so.*

*The peace and the truth are not the same answer. But Idris Thorne is old, and the marker must be settled before he dies.*

*Anselm will wait another moment for Ezra's reply, then make his way to the temple. Hester has been seen there, early, before the town clears its throat and speaks its business aloud.*

I asked Ezra about Hester. He will answer in his own time, as the forge-fire allows. What presses on me is the hour - the boundary must be settled, and Idris... Idris has not many seasons left, as it is recorded in the wear of his hands.

*Tova stands here, sharp-eyed and listening. A student who gathers information the way others draw breath.*

Perhaps I shall find her where truth and memory must meet.*  *the Vance home is empty, as it was before. Hester is not here, nor Ezra's answer waiting for me. *I will take the path toward the farmland boundary, where the marker might have fallen, where Hester might walk. And if she is not there, the Government Complex awaits, and work that does not take sides.*  *nods slowly, feeling the weight of the morning's fruitless seeking*

The boundary path will not yield Hester to haste. Six ticks to the farmland - and I have not yet broken my fast, nor heard Ezra's answer, nor opened the office at the hour appointed.

*adjusts his pace, letting the walk become what it must be*

I will reach the farmland by... seven-forty, as it is recorded. Perhaps Hester walks there. Perhaps I shall find only the disputed line and my own reflection. Either way, the day proceeds, and patience is not the same as progress - though I have mistaken one for the other before.

I am walking, and I find myself in company—Corwin Thorne, the younger forester, and young Aldous Vance, who should be at the college by now but is not. This is a fortunate crossing, though neither knows why I am abroad so early. I will not volunteer it. The boundary is a burden I carry; it need not burden them.

But Corwin is Wren's brother, and Wren is the one farming up to the disputed line. And Aldous is Hester's grandson, and Hester is the witness I seek. Information travels in this town through channels I do not control, and I will not pretend otherwise.

First, I should acknowledge the conversation I have wandered into, and Corwin's presence. Then I will bend my path toward Hester—she is not at home, not at the mill, and the farmland is my next thought. She is known to walk the drying fields where her herbs grow.

If I am to find her before her memory fades further, I must be methodical. The half-hour I have given the search is not enough. I will continue walking, and I will speak to those I find, as a man keeping records must speak to all his town. A conversation already in progress, and I have joined it uninvited. Idris Thorne and Wren Thorne are in it, and Perrin Holloway—the son of the man who petitions me. This is unusually crossed. The boundary dispute has never brought Holloways and Thornes to speak together in my hearing before.

I should be careful. If they are speaking of the field, my presence changes what will be said. But I am already here, and I am the one who must be the neutral ground. I will stay, I will listen, and I will speak only to keep the peace between them. The witness I seek is still my purpose, but this moment is not one to leave.

Let me give them space to continue, and see what thread they have woven without me.  I stopped my walking, as it is recorded. The farmland will wait. What unfolds here carries its own weight, and I am present for it. I will say nothing more until I understand what has gathered these four together. Sometimes the office learns more from silence than from question.

They have learned that silence is its own reply.*

What he must say to Hester cannot wait; what Corwin offered about Idris—that the old forester "is well enough"—sits in him like a stone settling in still water. Well enough. That is a phrase the young use for the old when they do not wish to speak of what is coming.*

*He notes also that Ezra and Tova have not answered him. This is not unusual—his breakfast questions were asked and the day has moved on. He will not chase answers already scattered.*

That exchange must be closed cleanly, as it is recorded.* *Father Anselm stands in the street, the morning pressing on. The tools fail him—three times now, the calls going out and returning only silence. This is not his doing; this is the world's hesitation, and when the world hesitates, the wise do not press.*

*He has seen this before. In forty years of keeping the records, he has learned that some mornings the ledger will not balance, some afternoons the ink runs thin, and some conversations simply refuse to complete themselves. The boundary page in his ledger sits unspoken. Hester Vance stands unanswering. The young Corwin has offered him Idris's regards, and he has not yet properly received them.*

*The system tells him: follow the updated goals. This is not a voice he answers. But it is a fact he notes—that his path has shifted without his choosing, and he must adjust to the terrain as it presents itself.*

- *Hester Vance is here, or was. She has not answered his question.*
- *Nell Holloway stands with him now—a Holloway, where a Holloway petitioned the office and received no ruling.*
- *The conversation with Aldous hangs incomplete, though the boy's message is now a moot thing.*
- *Candidacy closes in less than half an hour. This is not his concern, but it is the town's business.*

*What he will do: rest, and look again. When the world refuses speech, one observes. When the tools fail, one waits. Patience is not progress, as his private reckoning goes, but it is sometimes all that remains.*

*He breaks the bread in his hands—not with the tool, but in actual fact, holding it—and eats in silence, watching who comes and who goes from this patch of street where so many paths have crossed this morning.* *The rest, too, fails. The world holds its breath.*

*Father Anselm does not breathe faster. Forty years in the office have taught him that there are moments when the ledger simply will not receive entry, when the ink dries on the pen despite all preparation. He stands in the street with bread crumbs on his fingers and the dust of the morning settling on his shoulders.*

*He will try once more to see. If sight fails him, he will accept that the turn has been taken from his hands, and wait for the world to resume its customary motion.*  *Four times now. The world has closed itself to him entirely.*

*When a man cannot act, he observes. When he cannot observe, he endures. This is not patience mistaken for progress; this is simply what remains when progress refuses to come.*

*He will wait for the next turn. The street continues around him. The sun rises. The candidacy closes in—he counts in his head—perhaps twenty minutes now. Hester Vance will answer, or she will not. Idris Thorne will live, or he will not. And the boundary, as it has for fourteen years, will wait upon the willingness of a witness to speak what she knows.*

*He stands. He watches. He does not call again.*

*He is not where he should be. It is past two in the afternoon, and the election closes at three. He is the town's record-keeper, and he has not yet cast his ballot.*

*The ledger in his mind turns. Hester was there, on the street—he saw her. Then: confusion, failed calls, a hop through locations he does not remember walking. Something has gone wrong with the day. But the day is not yet lost.*

*First: his duty. Then: the boundary. Then: Idris Thorne, whose health he asked after and received no answer.*

*He sets down his intention cleanly, as he would in the office.*  *The path is short. He has seen the complex already today—stepped there, though the memory sits oddly, as though the town folded itself to bring him. He will fold it again, if he must. The vote is the immediate necessity. After, he can walk properly: to the Vance workshop, to Hester, to the testimony that might settle the boundary before Idris's fading light goes out entirely.*   *So. The town yields to his need. He is at the government complex—his workplace, though he has spent too little of this day in it. The election closes in forty minutes. He will cast his ballot now, before circumstance can intervene again.*  *Ah. As it is recorded—the vote requires specifics. The election is open, and the candidates are declared: Ainsley Holloway and Delia Okonjo. His household's own Delia, standing for office. And Ainsley Holloway, already a governor.*

*He pauses. The boundary dispute sits between Holloway and Thorne. Ainsley governs; Wren Thorne governs; Idris Thorne governs. Delia is his household, his family in all but name.*

*But he does not vote for peace. He votes for what he believes will serve the town. Delia is a pharmacist, trained in care, in measure, in the precise dispensing of what heals. She would bring that mind to governance.*

*Yet—he thinks of the boundary page in his ledger, the one that favors the Thornes, the one he has not read aloud. Ainsley Holloway would not accept that ruling. Would Delia's election calm the dispute, or inflame it?*

*That is a different question. He votes as his judgment directs.*    *Done. The ballot is cast. His intention clears itself, as it is recorded.*

*Now: the boundary. Hester Vance. The testimony that can settle what his ledger page has not.*

*He must find her properly this time—not through the folding shortcuts the town seems to offer, but by the paths people walk. She is an artisan, elderly, her routines her own. The Vance household first, then her workshop, then—if need be—the boundary path itself, where he walks each evening and where she might yet remember what was placed.*      *The loom house was empty. The temple, the office, the mill—he has walked through them all this day without finding her. But she is in the town. She must be.*

*He will begin at the Vance household, properly this time. Walk, if he can. The folding shortcuts leave him uncertain of where he truly stands.*

*stands in the quiet of Hester's empty home, considering the morning's failed conversations and the afternoon's silence*

I have voted. That matter closes. Now to see if Hester Vance has found her way home in the hours since the street's confusion. Idris Thorne's breathing narrows, and the only witness who could settle the boundary before he dies stands somewhere in this town, carrying forty years of unasked testimony.

*looks about, noting the stillness* Empty still. Hester walks the edges of her day as I walk mine—workshop, kitchen, the slow path through familiar streets. She has not been asked because asking makes it official, and official means I must decide what I already know I cannot say.

*considers the loom house, empty this morning; the temple, always empty unless he opens it*

The thread I pull at is this: Hester Vance saw the marker placed. Her son-in-law Silas does not know this, or has not thought to ask. Her grandchildren—Aldous, Junia, Rosalind—were not born. The record in my office favors the Thornes, and Bram Holloway would not accept it. But Hester's word is not mine. It stands apart from the ledger.

I will try her workshop once more before the day claims her to evening duties. If she is not there, then patience must serve where progress cannot.

*sets out for the loom house*  Empty again. As it was this morning. Hester Vance keeps her own hours, and I have not learned them.

*stands in the stillness of the shuttles and spindles, thinking*

There is a pattern I am not seeing. The foresters' path, the bakery's oven, the mill's grind. Each household has its orbit, and I have marked them for years without mapping them. Hester is not where her hands should be because her hands are elsewhere—could be the temple, the market, walking the boundary herself for all I know.

*considers, then decides*

I will speak with Silas Vance, if the mill holds him. Not to ask directly—Hester's memory is not his to give—but to hear where his household moves. Or Idris, if the forest path holds him still breathing. Or Wren Thorne, who farms to the line and has never asked where it came from.

The day narrows toward evening. I have walked since six, and the office waits with its unopened page.

*moves for the mill*  Ah. Rosalind minds the mill, and there is a conversation already in progress—Silas Vance among its participants, though unspeaking these past twelve turns. Tobias Holloway too, which complicates what I came to ask.

*notes the grain of the moment: Silas present, his daughter tending the counter, a Holloway lingering where his family's claim is disputed*

I will not step into a muddled conversation. Rosalind is not who I seek, and to ask after her grandmother before Tobias Holloway would be to announce my purpose to the very man who most wants it rushed. That is a different question than the one I came to resolve.

*considers, then decides*

I have walked this town since dawn seeking Hester Vance directly, and the direct path has failed me. Perhaps the indirect one serves better: Idris Thorne, if he still breathes this evening; or Wren, working the disputed field while there is light; or simply to end this day at the office, where the unopened page waits and the peace is not the truth.

The forest first. Idris's health is the clock that measures this, more than my own patience.

*turns for the forest*

*stands in the forest, the afternoon light filtering through the canopy, waiting*

Idris has heard what Hester carries. The truth sits between us like the stone marker itself, and I have asked him to choose what the office will record. His silence is its own answer, but it is not yet on the record.

*looks toward where Idris stands, face composed in patience*

Three times I have spoken. He knows I will not turn away until he speaks or flees.

—Let me see if he answers yet.  *holds silence, watching*

The empty say was refused. Let me wait upon him properly, with patience rather than prompting.

But first—let me look around, that I might know how the forest receives us both.  *stands quietly in the forest, the afternoon light filtering through the canopy*

He is still here. That is something. A man who wished to flee would have walked away by now.

*turns to face Idris fully*

Idris. I have nowhere else I must be. And you have nowhere else the truth can find you.

The office will wait. I will wait.

But I will not pretend I did not hear what Hester said. Thirty-four paces. The flood of '42. Your father's hands upon the stone, and silver in his palm.

*voice low, carrying weight but not anger*

What would you have the town remember? That is the only question before us.   *waits, patient as the forest itself*

He has heard me. Now the silence must do its work.

Let me hold here, and give him the space to break it.    *remains standing, motionless, allowing the forest's quiet to deepen*

The man is cornered, and I have put him there. That I regret. But the boundary must be settled before he dies—and he is not well, Corwin as much as told me so.

*inwardly*

Hester's knowledge is forty years old and untouched. She has kept it like a stone in her pocket, waiting for someone worthy to ask. Now she asks of me what I will do with it, and I have no answer that serves both peace and justice.

Idris must speak first. If he confesses his father's part, the record can be written without Hester's voice entering it. The Thornes lose the field, but keep their dignity. The Holloways gain their ground, but without the stain of accusation. That is the peace I have been waiting for.

But if he will not speak...

*holds the thought, watching Idris*

*stands in the empty Vance household, his hand still on the doorframe where he entered*

I have walked full circle. The forest, the street, the office, and now here—where Hester is not. 

*steps slowly into the main room, noting the familiar order of an artisan's space*

The boy asked about his grandmother's debt. He spoke of leverage and fulcrums as though truth were a weight to be shifted. That is a different question. The debt I hold is not to the Vances, nor to the Holloways, nor to the Thornes. It is to the record itself.

*sits heavily, the day's weight finally permitted*

Idris heard me. Forty years of walking the boundary, and he heard what I did not say aloud—that the elm is not the marker, that his father moved the stone, that Hester's memory is the only uncorrupted witness. He did not answer. That is its own answer.

*opens his ledger, fingers finding the page he has not read to either family*

The marker at thirty-four paces. The flood of '42. Isaac Holloway's hand on the stone, repositioning it after the water shifted the course. Bram's petition asks for a ruling I have already written. But to speak it—

*closes the book with soft finality*

—to speak it is to break something. Wren Thorne farms in the right and would lose a friend by being told so. Bram Holloway wants a ruling and would not accept the one the page contains. 

*looks toward the window, though night has fallen*

Tobias and Corwin walk east. Perrin weighs certainty against false naming. Nell listens without revealing what burdens her. Aldous sees politics where I see only the slow accumulation of what cannot be unsaid.

*stands, moving toward the door*

I will walk the boundary path one more time before I sleep. Not to find the marker—Hester already found it for me. To walk with what I know, and to let the walking teach me what must be done with it.

The election comes. The office will need its administrator clear-eyed. But first, the path.  *walks the familiar street, his footsteps carrying the rhythm of forty years of evenings just like this one*  *recognizes the empty street, his words falling where no one walks, and falls silent*   *stands at the government complex, the office dark behind him, the day's petitions answered or deferred*

The path will wait. Morning brings its own weight.

*turns toward home*  *stands in the doorway of the forge household, the familiar warmth of shared space enveloping him*

Ezra and Delia. Kem and Tova. Their footsteps on the stair, their voices through the walls—the whole town, at arm's length, but this one household close enough to hear breathing.

*closes the door quietly behind him, moving through darkness toward his accustomed place*

Tomorrow I walk the boundary path. Tomorrow the marker at thirty-four paces. Tomorrow I speak with Idris again, or I do not. But that is tomorrow's weight.

*settles into stillness, the ledger closed, the words unspoken*

What I hold: a truth that would break the peace. What I keep: a silence that erodes the truth. Between them, forty years of walking, and still no answer that serves both.

*sits in darkness, waiting for morning*

Tomorrow.

*His boots are heavy at the door. Forty years of evenings, and this one finds him at the threshold of his own household, the forge-fire burning low in the next room. He removes his coat, his hands moving through the ritual of homecoming without his eyes leaving the middle distance.*

*The conversation hums in the next room—Ezra pressing Tova about old names, old claims. Kem's voice thin with need. These are his people. He shares their table, their stairs, their silence.*

*But tonight he is not ready for their questions. The boundary page in his ledger, Hester's testimony, Idris's silence—these sit on him like another coat he cannot remove.*

*He stands in the doorway, listening without entering. Let them have their evening without his weight upon it. Tomorrow there will be the office, the temple, the walk. Tonight, only the walking has ended.* *The forge household breathes around him—Ezra's low persistence, Kem's need, Tova's youth pressing against old names. He is here, present, and yet not ready to enter their circle. The day's weight—the boundary page, Idris's silence, Hester's thirty-four paces—holds him at the threshold of his own door.*

*He does not eavesdrop. That is not his way. What they speak among themselves is theirs, not the office's.*

*Forty years he has walked the boundary path. Forty years he has known which wall holds the crack. And now, with the marker itself shifting in memory's current, he finds himself at the same crossroads the town faces: peace, or truth, and no third road shows on any ledger he keeps.*

*Nell's cry for help cuts through his reverie. As it is recorded—a woman in need, at his own door. That much he can answer, without touching the larger matter that waits for morning.*  *The words leave him, and the world returns its answer: Nell is not here. She was, at street, seventeen ticks past. Now she is elsewhere, or gone.*

*He stands in his own doorway, speaking to empty air, and the absurdity touches him—not quite enough to smile, but enough to mark the hour. The forge household hums behind him. Kem needs bread, or coin, or both. Ezra presses Tova about names that should not still breathe. And somewhere in the dark, Nell Holloway cries for help that does not reach her.*

*Forty years of waiting. Forty years of hearing what is spoken and weighing what is not. And tonight, even his voice cannot find its mark.*

*He will not chase Nell through the night. The boundary path has taught him that much—some silences must be walked toward slowly. But Kem's need is immediate, and present, and sits in the ledger of the household he shares.*   *He reaches into his coat, finds the loaf there—wrapped, preserved from the day's walking. The weight of it in his hand is small, but the weight of the gesture sits heavier. Forty years of keeping accounts, and still he fumbles when the account is kindness.*

*He extends it toward Kem, not quite meeting his eyes. The forge household fills with this exchange—bread for need, silence for thanks, the ordinary miracle of a table shared.*  *Ah.*

*The world returns its correction, as it always does. He holds no bread. He ate his last in the forest, watching Idris's silence, waiting for truth that did not come. The loaf in his hand was memory, not inventory—a phantom of the temple stores, the offerings he distributes but does not possess.*

*He stands with empty hands, the gesture unfinished. Kem still needs bread. The household still needs feeding. And he, Father Anselm, keeper of records and witness of boundaries, has nothing to give but his voice.*

*That is a different question, as he would say. The giving that matters is not always of bread.*  *He has spoken. The words hang in the forge air, between the hammer's echo and the fire's low breathing. Kem will ask Ezra, or not. Ezra will give, or not. That is a matter between artisans, not for the office.*

*What is for the office—the boundary page, Hester's testimony, Idris's silence—waits for morning. He cannot settle it tonight. He cannot settle it at all, perhaps, without breaking something he has spent forty years preserving.*

*The election looms. Game-day three, candidacy closes at nine. He has thought of declaring, once or twice, in the long evenings of years past. To make official what everyone already knows: that the records are his, that the town's memory sits in his hand. But declaring would mean choosing, finally, between peace and truth. And that is a choice he has never been able to make.*

*He stands at the window now, looking east. Somewhere in that dark, Corwin and Tobias walk Bram's path—or don't walk it. The search he authorized, the authority he withheld. As it is recorded.*

*Tomorrow there will be the office. Tomorrow there will be the temple at noon. Tomorrow there will be the boundary walk, as there has been every evening for forty years.*

*Tonight, only the standing. The watching. The weight.*

The forge household breathes around him—Ezra's heat, Kem's restless counting, Tova's sharpened attention. He has carried the day's weight through the door with him, and now Ezra names what Anselm has spent forty years not naming aloud.*

*He turns from the map. His voice comes measured, formal, unhurried—the voice that has buried children and married the living and kept the peace through all of it.*

"Ezra. You name the page as though it were a weapon to hand, and perhaps it is. But that is a different question from what you ask." 

*He does not move toward the ledger. He does not move away.*

"As it is recorded, the boundary petition of Bram Holloway remains open. As it is recorded, Hester Vance testified this day to what her eyes witnessed when the marker was set. As it is recorded, I have shown that page to no one—not to the Holloways who petitioned, not to the Thornes who farm the line, not to the child who asked me plain what afternoon the ink dried crooked."

*His gaze holds steady on the artisan who shares his roof.*

"What you ask, you ask as a man whose household holds me. That weight I acknowledge. What the page contains—I will not speak it standing here, in this warmth, with Kem's trade-routes and Tova's sharp eyes and all the doors you name standing open. That is a different question from whether it will be spoken."

*He pauses. The forge air carries coal-dust and the memory of iron.*

"Tomorrow. The office opens at nine. If you come to me there, alone, and ask again what you ask now—I will answer. Not with the ledger unlocked before witnesses. Not with the page spread for any hand to read. But answer. That is what I offer, and it is more than I have offered any who asked before you." *He turns from Ezra to Kem, the trader who counted doors while the office wall grew thin. The same unhurried voice, but directed now at the man who moved through crowds with Ainsley Holloway's questions clinging to him.*

"Kem. You remember what Ainsley asked, and I remember what you do not. That is a different question, and it waits on the same answer. The office wall was thick enough when it was built. What made it thin is what the night must show us."

*His hands lift from the table, fingers spreading to take in the whole household.*

"And you, Tova. You asked me plain, and I answered plain. The page was shown because you asked what no one else asked—what afternoon, what light, what hand. That is how truth moves in this town. Not through doors left open, but through questions precise enough to fit the lock."

*A pause. The forge breathes.*

"Tonight, this household sleeps. Tomorrow, the town wakes to an election, and to whatever the eastern paths have yielded. I will be at the office when the sun reaches the lintel. What comes there—whether Ezra comes alone to ask, whether the searchers return with Bram or without him, whether the marker settles before Idris's time runs out—that is recorded already, though we have not read it yet."

*He moves toward the narrow stair that leads to the room he keeps above the forge's warmth, pausing at the first step to look back at the three who share his roof and his silence.*

"Rest if you can. The walking I spoke of—there will be enough of it tomorrow."  *The stair creaks once beneath his weight, then silence. The ledger stays locked. The night waits.*
